title: Hartman Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Hartman wells have a 119 ft median depth; typical completed well costs are $10,200-$18,500.
h1: Hartman, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Well records within 5 miles of Hartman show a mostly shallow plains setting, but the spread is wide. The median reported depth is 119 feet, and the middle half runs from 65 to 162 feet. Many permits are for irrigation, stock, or monitoring rather than household water, so a nearby well is useful evidence but not a guarantee for a homesite.

This page uses Colorado Division of Water Resources permit records, including 249 wells, of which 154 are recorded as constructed. Only 30 report a pump yield and only 1 reports a static water level. Treat the local numbers as planning information, then confirm the site with a driller and the state permit file.

sections.heading: Hartman well depths and the plains geology
sections.html:
Hartman wells are commonly shallow. Records put 45% under 100 feet and another 46% between 100 and 300 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 272 feet, while the deepest record reaches 1,094 feet. That range matters when comparing drilling bids: a bid based only on the 119-foot median may not cover an unusually deep hole.

The records identify 226 wells with an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, along with 14 in the Ogallala and 3 in the Dakota Sandstone. Hartman sits on plains alluvium and sedimentary rock, so local material, the target aquifer, casing, and grout requirements can change the final design.

sections.heading: How much water Hartman wells produce
sections.html:
The reported yield numbers are unusually strong, but they come from only 30 wells. The median reported yield is 650 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 16.2 to 1,209 gallons per minute. The records show 77% of reported wells at 15 gallons per minute or more, and 23% between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

No reported well falls under 5 gallons per minute in this dataset. That does not mean every new domestic well will produce that much. The sample includes a large irrigation share, and irrigation wells can be designed and tested differently from household wells. Ask for the completion report and pumping test for nearby domestic wells before relying on the high median.

sections.heading: Hartman water levels and what the records show
sections.html:
Only 1 well reports a static water level, so the available water-level evidence is very limited. Its reported depth to water is 50 feet, and the listed median and middle-half figures are also 50 feet. That single observation cannot establish a water-table trend for Hartman, Granada, or nearby properties.

The permit history does not provide a decade-by-decade water-level series. It therefore cannot support a claim that groundwater is falling or stable. A driller can check nearby completion records, and a buyer should ask for a recent measurement from the property or neighboring wells. Water level, pumping drawdown, and seasonal conditions are separate questions.

sections.heading: Hartman permit history and the drillers in the records
sections.html:
Hartman-area permits span the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2020. The busiest decades in the supplied records were the 2000s with 41 permits, followed by the 2010s with 27. The 1960s had 25, while the 1990s had 22.

The most frequently listed drillers are Ark Valley Pump & Supply (Smith Jr., William), with 25 records; Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 22; and Ark Valley Pump & Supply (Smith, William David), with 18. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation or proof of current availability. Check the current permit status and talk with a licensed driller before scheduling work.

sections.heading: What a new Hartman well may cost
sections.html:
For Hartman’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the supplied drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the local median depth of 119 feet, that puts the drilled hole at about $4,200-$6,500. This is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $10,200-$18,500. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, casing or grout changes, water treatment, or an unusual pump setup can move the price. Get the bid in writing and ask what footage, casing, testing, electrical, trenching, and restoration are included.

sections.heading: Hartman risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. The records include 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1 historic mine-features site, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within about 10 miles. These mapped sites do not establish contamination at a particular parcel, but they are a reason to review environmental records and test the water after closing.

Also verify septic setbacks, the proposed home location, driveway access, and room for a well-service truck. Colorado DWR permits control how a well may be used. Household-use wells are commonly exempt wells, but the permit conditions still matter, and the general exempt-well pumping limit is 35 gallons per minute. A new build may also need an augmentation plan in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: Buying land near Hartman, Granada, and Holly
sections.html:
Before buying, pull the closest well permits and separate domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells. Hartman’s records are 57% irrigation, 16% stock, 17% monitoring, and 12% domestic or household. That mix explains why a large reported yield should not be treated as a household guarantee.

Have a local driller review the parcel, access, likely depth, aquifer target, and neighboring completions before you remove a well contingency. For context, Granada is 6 miles away, Holly is 7 miles, and Lamar is 22 miles; those areas can provide additional records, but geology and permitted use still need to be checked at the actual lot.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Hartman, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported Hartman well depth is 119 feet, with the middle half from 65 to 162 feet. Records show 45% under 100 feet and 46% from 100 to 300 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,094 feet, so a buyer should not assume the median depth applies to every parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Hartman?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 119-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $4,200-$6,500. A completed system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $10,200-$18,500. Access, depth, casing, grout, and pump requirements can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Hartman wells produce?
faq.a: Only 30 wells report a pump yield, so the yield sample is limited. The median reported yield is 650 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 16.2 to 1,209 gallons per minute. The records show 77% at 15 gallons per minute or more, but many wells are irrigation wells rather than household wells.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Hartman, Colorado?
faq.a: The permit map shows 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, plus 1 historic mine-features site and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those locations do not prove contamination at your property. Test the well water after purchase or construction and review environmental records before relying on it for household use.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Hartman?
faq.a: The supplied records cannot show a reliable trend. Only 1 well reports a static water level, listed at 50 feet, so there is no useful water-level-by-decade series. Have a driller check nearby records and measure the property or neighboring wells. Static level and pumping drawdown should be evaluated separately.
